answer.question: Do I need a Certificate of Appropriateness for artificial turf in Springfield?
answer.answer: Possibly. Jacksonville's code requires one before any alteration or new construction on property in a historic district. It exempts routine lawn and landscape care only when no hardscape is added or changed, and it defines hardscape as any non-vegetative element of landscaping. Turf isn't named either way. Before work starts, ask the City's Historic Preservation Section whether your layout, edging and any pavers need a COA.

blocks.h2: In Springfield, the permission comes before the dig.
paras: Springfield has its own zoning overlay. Ordinance 2000-302-E adopted it, and every parcel inside is subject to the Springfield Historic District Regulations (Ord. Code 656.367). Its edge follows Hogans Creek, Broad Street and the old Seaboard Coast Line rail line, so check your address first.

Inside it, Jacksonville's preservation chapter requires a Certificate of Appropriateness, or COA, before any alteration, new construction, demolition or relocation, on top of any building permit you need. The COA's conditions are written into that permit, and work started without one can be stopped with a notice of violation (Ord. Code 307.106).

SPAR, Springfield's preservation group, says every property in the district needs one before exterior changes, and lists fences, sidewalks, driveways and curb cuts alongside roofs and windows (SPAR design rules).

blocks.h2: The code exempts lawn care, not hardscape. Turf sits in between.
paras: You don't need a COA for routine lawn and landscape care or maintenance. That exemption leaves out changes to existing hardscape and new hardscape (Ord. Code 307.107). The code defines hardscape as any non-vegetative element of landscaping, especially masonry or woodwork, and names retaining walls, driveways, parking pads, patios, walkways, decks, trellises, arbors, pergolas and water fountains (Ord. Code 307.102).

Artificial turf isn't alive, and it isn't on that list, so the code doesn't settle which side it falls on. The pieces around it are easier to place: a paver border, a concrete mow strip or a new path to the dog run look a lot like the named examples.

So ask the City's Historic Preservation Section two questions, in writing. Does this layout need a COA? Can staff approve it without a hearing? Take the drawing from our free visit with you, and see our permit guide for what to ask about the dig itself.

blocks.h2: Minor work can be signed off by staff. Major work waits for a hearing.
paras: The Historic Preservation Commission keeps a list of routine alterations and minor work that City staff can approve without a public hearing, if the work follows the district's design regulations (Ord. Code 307.107). SPAR points owners to the City's COA Matrix, which sorts work into staff approvals and Commission votes.

If yours goes to the Commission, build the wait into your plans. The completed application has to be filed at least 21 calendar days before the meeting. You post signs along every street side of the lot, no more than 200 feet apart, at least 14 days before the hearing. The Commission decides within 30 days after the hearing, and the signed order follows within 15 calendar days (Ord. Code 307.106).

Once it's approved, the clock runs the other way. A COA expires 12 months after it's issued if the work hasn't started, and five years after it's issued if the work isn't finished, unless the Commission extends it (Ord. Code 307.106). A staff approval can be appealed to the Commission within 21 days (Ord. Code 307.107), so ask staff whether to wait out that window before you book the install.

blocks.kicker: Small lots, close to the street
blocks.h2: Springfield lots are narrow, so the front yard is always on show.
paras: In the RMD-S residential district, a single-family lot can be as narrow as 25 feet and as small as 2,500 square feet. The front setback is a 10-foot minimum and a 15-foot maximum, and the rear setback is ten feet. Buildings and structures can cover at most 50 percent of the lot (Ord. Code 656.368). If your plan adds a deck or other structure next to the turf, ask the City how it counts toward that cap.

That adds up to a shallow front yard facing the street and a compact yard out back. When the Commission reviews new construction, one of its criteria is that landscaping be compatible with the character of the house and the houses around it (Ord. Code 307.106). A pet area behind the back fence and turf across the front yard may not get the same answer, so if you want both, ask about both.

blocks.h2: Look up the trees and your neighbors' approvals before you pick a layout.
paras: SPAR notes that many trees in the district are protected and need special permits before they come out. Plan the turf around a tree rather than removing it to make room, and read how turf works under a tree before you set the edge.

COAs are public records. In the City's Land Use & Zoning Portal, choose Inquire Application, then Show Advanced Search, to look one up by address, your neighbors' included. The JaxGIS Land Development Review maps confirm whether a property is in the district, and SPAR's Design Review Committee of planners, architects and engineers offers technical help (SPAR).

servicesNote: Compare a front-yard lawn, a pet area behind the fence or a small green, and take the layout to the City before the install is booked.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Springfield, FL?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, pet turf and backyard putting greens in Springfield, FL. Here the first question is whether the City must issue a Certificate of Appropriateness for your layout, so our free visit gives you a measured, custom layout to take to the Historic Preservation Section. Call 303-349-2368 to set it up.

faq.q: Doesn't Florida law stop the City from blocking turf?
faq.a: Since the state's turf standard took effect on May 19, 2026 (Rule 62-308.100), a local government can't prohibit compliant turf on a single-family lot of 1 acre or less, or regulate it inconsistently with that standard (Fla. Stat. 125.572). The statute never mentions historic districts or certificates of appropriateness, and Jacksonville's COA rule is still in the code. Nothing we found settles how the two fit together, so ask the Historic Preservation Section. Our Florida turf guide covers the standard.

faq.q: Does a non-contributing house still need a COA?
faq.a: Yes. SPAR says contributing houses, non-contributing houses and new construction in the district all need a COA before exterior work begins; the design guidelines are just stricter for contributing structures. The City's list of contributing and non-contributing properties is searchable by address.

faq.q: What happens if the work starts without a COA?
faq.a: The Planning and Development Department can issue a notice of violation that stops all work, and work that strays from an approved COA can be stopped the same way (Ord. Code 307.106). The City's Municipal Code Compliance Division also inspects properties to confirm they match an approved COA.
